A small change inside a well-made cell can alter the course of human health, and that idea is what drew me toward biotechnology. I am from India, and I hold a Bachelor’s degree from a university not listed in the major global rankings. What first made this field feel personal was seeing how closely my interest in science and my family’s progress shaped how I see the role of medical research. During a family visit, I once explained one of my projects by using kitchen ingredients to mimic a lab experiment, and a casual conversation turned into an enthusiastic mini science lesson around the dining table. That moment stayed with me because it captured how closely my interest in approachable science meets practical work. I am especially drawn to biotech research because it combines curiosity, careful investigation, and the chance to connect science with human impact in meaningful ways.

Through my studies and project work, I have developed a practical approach to laboratory work and to the complex processes involved. In one role, I needed to use a new technique that the work required; within a couple of months I had learned it well enough to apply it independently in my own tasks. On another project, a recurring issue was slowing the team down, so I put together a practical workaround that reduced the disruption and helped the work move forward more smoothly. I have also completed 5 projects with tangible outcomes, each reinforcing the importance of carrying work through to a clear result.

In addition, colleagues now and then come to me with questions in areas they know I have worked on, and I value those exchanges because they help keep work collaborative and focused. During a long assignment that included setbacks and revisions, I kept the work moving over an extended period and put in extra time when needed to bring it to completion. Through this, I have strengthened my communication, organisation, teamwork, and research habits. Looking ahead, I am eager to bring this foundation to a Biotech Research Assistant role and contribute reliable, well-supported work that supports meaningful research and patient outcomes.

One of my favourite memories is sitting at the kitchen table with a family member, assembling simple reading-game resources, then hearing later that the class had asked to play them again the very next day. That moment captured for me how teaching can reach beyond the classroom and become something others feel connected to as well. Originally from Colombia, I hold a Master’s degree from a university ranked in the global top 500, and across my work I have completed 5 projects with tangible outcomes.

My academic and professional path has strengthened my commitment to creating engaging, inclusive lessons that respond to different learning styles while keeping the classroom calm, positive, and purposeful. In one role, I needed to use a new teaching tool and became comfortable with it within a few months of focused effort, which allowed me to contribute to day-to-day planning and lesson delivery. On another occasion, I noticed that the team was repeatedly losing time at the same stage of a recurring process, so I introduced a simple adjustment to the process that reduced delays and saved time across the group. Colleagues now and then come to me with questions in areas they know I have worked on, and I value those moments because they reflect the collaborative side of teaching.

What keeps this profession personal for me is the human side of it. One of my favourite family memories is of a younger relative who ran straight to a classroom display and began explaining the different stages of a game like a teacher before I said a word; that moment captured exactly why I want to keep contributing to primary education. I am now eager to bring my background, practical experience, and commitment to inclusive, engaging learning into a Primary School Teacher role.
